title: Using method references with functional interfaces

blocks.text: 4.3.3. Using Method References with Functional Interfaces
A teammate adds one method to `Customer`, beside the one that was already there:

String displayName() { return name; }
String displayName(Locale locale) { return name.toUpperCase(locale); }
Their branch compiles. The next build fails in a file they never opened, on a line that has sorted customers for two years:
customers.sort(Comparator.comparing(Customer::displayName).reversed());

Customers.java:12: error: incompatible types: cannot infer type-variable(s) T,U
        customers.sort(Comparator.comparing(Customer::displayName).reversed());
                                           ^
    (argument mismatch; invalid method reference
      incompatible types: Object cannot be converted to Locale)

Nothing on that line passes a `Locale`. javac picks which `displayName` the reference names from the parameter types the functional interface supplies, and here it supplied none. Five rules follow, one per heading. Every output is from javac and Java 21.
The Interface's Parameter Types Choose the Overload; the Value at Run Time Doesn't
`String.valueOf` has nine overloads, among them `valueOf(char[])` and `valueOf(Object)`. Before reading the output, decide what each reference prints for the same array:

A-7 | [C@7f31245a
null
Cannot read the array length because "value" is null

javac resolves `String::valueOf` like the call `String.valueOf(x)`, with `x` typed `char[]` in one and `Object` in the other. That happens once, at compile time: `javap -v` shows one reference pointing at `String.valueOf:([C)Ljava/lang/String;` and the other at `String.valueOf:(Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/String;`. From then on `fromObject` calls `valueOf(Object)` whatever it is given, and for an array that means `toString()`, the class name and a hash. A `null` goes the other way: `valueOf(Object)` writes `"null"`, and `valueOf(char[])` throws.
An export that keeps its column formatters as `Function<Object, String>` therefore writes `[C@7f31245a` into a token column, and a test suite whose tokens are all `String`s never sees it.
javac searches in the same phases as for a call: first without boxing, then with it, then varargs. `Math::max` has `int`, `long`, `float` and `double` overloads:

9 9 9
boxed.apply(null, 9): java.lang.NullPointerException
-2147483648 2147483648

No `max(Integer, Integer)` exists, so for `BinaryOperator<Integer>` javac allows unboxing, finds all four overloads applicable, and takes the most specific, `max(int, int)`. The reference unboxes each argument before the call, so a `null` element throws a `NullPointerException` with no message. With `abs` the overload changes the answer: `Integer.MIN_VALUE` has no positive `int`, so `abs(int)` returns it unchanged, while `abs(long)` returns 2147483648.

For an unbound reference the interface's first parameter is the receiver, and it may be any subtype of the class before `::`: `Function<String, String> show = Object::toString` compiles. The other way round fails, since an `Object` is not a `String`: `Function<Object, Integer> length = String::length` gives `method length in class String cannot be applied to given types`.
<!-- practice 1 -->
An Exact Reference Lets javac Pick `submit(Callable)`; Overloading the Method Makes the Call Ambiguous
`ExecutorService.submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` and `Callable<T>`. A method that returns a value fits both, since a `Runnable` can drop the result. Which does each line choose?

submit(this::refresh).get() = 120
submit(this::clear).get()   = null

`refresh` has one declaration, is not generic and takes no varargs, so javac knows the call `this::refresh` makes before it chooses between the `submit`s. Such a reference is *exact*. Both fit, and the one whose method returns a value is more specific: the same preference unit 4.1.2 showed for lambdas. `clear` returns `void` and fits only `Runnable`.
Now the price cache gets a second `refresh`:

PriceCache.java:8: error: reference to submit is ambiguous
        return pool.submit(this::refresh);
                   ^
  both method <T>submit(Callable<T>) in ExecutorService and method submit(Runnable) in ExecutorService match

Which `refresh` the reference names now depends on the target. The reference is *inexact*, and javac doesn't use it to choose the overload of `submit`: it only checks that some `refresh` takes as many arguments as each candidate's interface supplies. Both pass and neither is more specific, so the call is ambiguous. A single varargs method (`int count(String... names)`) or generic method (`static <T> T none()`) gave javac 21 the same error. Naming the target fixes one call site:

System.out.println("cast:   " + pool.submit((Callable<Integer>) cache::refresh).get());
System.out.println("lambda: " + pool.submit(() -> cache.refresh()).get());

cast:   120
lambda: 120
The lambda has no parameters, so its body can be checked against both overloads, and the value-returning one wins.
An Inexact Method Reference Leaves Inference Without the Types It Needs

Back to the opening. `comparing` is generic, `<T, U> Comparator<T> comparing(Function<? super T, ? extends U>)`. Assigned straight to a `Comparator<Customer>`, it gets `T` from the target. With `.reversed()` called on its result it gets no target (unit 4.1.3), and `T` must come from the argument. While `displayName` had one declaration, the reference told inference its types: the receiver is a `Customer`, the key a `String`. Once overloaded, it tells inference nothing. `T` becomes `Object`, and javac then reports the closest candidate it tried, `displayName(Locale)` with an `Object` argument.
`String::toLowerCase`, overloaded with `toLowerCase(Locale)`, fails the same way:

Lower.java:4: error: incompatible types: cannot infer type-variable(s) T,U
    Comparator<String> zToA = Comparator.comparing(String::toLowerCase).reversed();
                                                  ^
    (argument mismatch; invalid method reference
      incompatible types: Object cannot be converted to Locale)

`comparing(String::length).reversed()` compiles, because `length` has one declaration. Unit 4.1.3's advice, use a method reference where a lambda can't infer its parameter, holds only for exact references. Each of these sorts `Mei`, `Ade` and `Zora`:

[Zora, Mei, Ade]
[Zora, Mei, Ade]
[Zora, Mei, Ade]
The first is the one to prefer: `comparing` gets its target from `sort`, and the order to reverse is the key's.
A Generic Method Needs Type Arguments When Nothing Else Gives Them
`Collections::emptyList` names one method, but its `T` is open until a target fixes it. In a chain, nothing does:

CompletableFuture<List<String>> names =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Collections::emptyList).thenApply(list -> list);

EmptyChain.java:6: error: incompatible types: inference variable U has incompatible bounds
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Collections::emptyList).thenApply(list -> list);
                                                                           ^
    equality constraints: List<String>
    lower bounds: List<Object>
`supplyAsync` inferred a `List<Object>`, and `thenApply` can't turn it into a `List<String>`. `Collections::<String>emptyList` supplies the type argument, and the same chain compiles and yields `[]`.

**javac and the specification.** As we read JLS 15.13.1, a generic method reference with explicit type arguments is exact. javac 21 still reports `pool.submit(Collections::<String>emptyList)` as ambiguous, like `this::refresh`; a cast to `Callable<List<String>>` compiles.
A Varargs Method Packs the Interface's Arguments, So an Array Becomes One Element

`String.format(String, Object...)` fits a `BiFunction<String, Object, String>`. No `format(String, Object)` exists, so javac reaches the varargs phase and compiles the reference to a synthetic `lambda$` method (unit 4.3.1) that calls `String.format(t, x)` with `x` typed `Object`, so `x` is packed into a new one-element array. A routing service renders shard names this way:

direct:    eu-west/7
reference: shard eu-west
reference: java.util.MissingFormatArgumentException: Format specifier '%s'
reference: true
spread:    eu-west/7

The direct call passes its `Object[]` as the varargs array. Through the reference the array arrives typed `Object` and is packed: the first `%s` gets the whole array, printed as `[Ljava.lang.Object;@…`, and the second finds nothing. Single values work, so the failure appears with the first message that carries two. With `Object[]` as the parameter type, the reference passes the array through.
A primitive array is never spread into `T...`, since an `int[]` is not an `Object[]`:
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Method That Throws a Checked Exception Doesn't Fit `Function`
`Files.readString(Path)` declares `throws IOException`, and `Function.apply` declares nothing:

The rule is the one for a lambda's body, but a reference has no body to put a `try` in. Unit 3.2.2 gives the two ways out: a functional interface whose method declares the exception, which takes `Files::readString` as it is, or a lambda that wraps the exception and code at your boundary that unwraps it.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **The interface's parameter types choose the overload, at compile time.** `String::valueOf` as a `Function<Object, String>` prints `[C@…` for a `char[]`; `Math::abs` as an `IntUnaryOperator` leaves `Integer.MIN_VALUE` negative; a boxed target unboxes and throws on `null`.

**An exact reference (one declaration, not generic, not varargs) lets javac pick `submit(Callable)`.** Adding an overload makes every `submit(this::m)` ambiguous; a cast or a lambda fixes the call site.
**An inexact reference leaves inference without the types it needs.** `comparing(m).reversed()` breaks when `m` gains an overload; pass `reverseOrder()` to `comparing`, or give type arguments.
**A varargs method packs the interface's arguments.** An `Object[]` passed as `Object` becomes one element, and an `int[]` is never spread.
**A checked exception doesn't fit `Function`.** Use an interface that declares it, or wrap it in a lambda (unit 3.2.2).

blocks.text: Reference
**Which method a reference names (javac 21, handles read with `javap -v`):**

rows: `max(int, int)`; the boxed target throws on `null`
`format(String, Object...)`, argument packed into a new array
`asList(T...)` with `T = int[]`: a list of one

rows: `incompatible thrown types IOException in functional expression`
`method length in class String cannot be applied to given types`

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Pick a class in your codebase that other modules use through method references. Which of its methods could gain an overload without breaking a caller's build, and how would you find out before merging?

Your API takes a `Function<Object, String>` formatter, and callers pass `String::valueOf`. Would you change the parameter type, add overloads for common types, or document it? What does each cost a caller?

`submit(this::refresh)` and `submit(() -> refresh())` both choose `Callable` today. Which one keeps compiling when `refresh` gains an overload, and which one would you write in a code base you don't control?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why javac Ignores an Overloaded Reference While It Picks an Overload

To choose an overload of `submit`, javac checks every argument against every candidate. For a reference to an overloaded method, that would mean resolving the reference again for each candidate's parameter types, and each resolution could pick a different method, while the candidate's own type variables would depend on that pick. javac leaves such a reference out of the choice and resolves it once, against the method chosen. The cost lands on callers: adding an overload doesn't break compiled ones (a `Scheduler` compiled against the old `PriceCache` still printed `get() = 120` against the new one), but breaks them at their next compile.
